meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

items.whyNow: The Kremlin's 24 Sep rejection of a 'temporary settlement' leaves the energy-strike truce Zelensky offered at the UN dead for now, so both sides' deep-strike campaigns run into winter unchecked, while Vivaldi's second phase shows robot-borne logistics and air-delivered ground robots sustaining a local counteroffensive.
changes: 25 Sep: Ukrainian drones reportedly set the Perm refinery (~1,500 km from the border) ablaze and hit the Iskra electronics plant in Ulyanovsk; not yet confirmed by Ukraine's General Staff (Kyiv Independent, single source).

24 Sep: Russia launched 282 attack drones plus Zircon, Iskander-M, S-400 and KN-23 missiles in three ballistic waves; two killed and eight injured in Kyiv, a maternity hospital damaged; 227 targets downed including 219 drones, 4 Zircons and 3 ballistic missiles, which Zelensky put at 60% of ballistic missiles over Kyiv (Kyiv Independent, Meduza).

24 Sep: Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Moscow seeks 'peace, not a temporary ceasefire', which ISW assessed as an effective rejection of the US–Ukrainian limited energy ceasefire (New Voice of Ukraine, ISW via Kyiv Post).

24 Sep: Suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania (Solca, Suceava county, after four minutes in its airspace) and Moldova (a camera-equipped Gerbera in Floresti); Romania said a protest to Moscow was required; on 23 Sep a Russian Mi-8 entered Polish airspace near Braniewo for 42 seconds and jets were scrambled (Kyiv Independent, Euronews).
24 Sep: Finnish President Stubb publicly pleaded with Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage over Russia and occupied Ukraine so Ukraine can strike ballistic missile launchers (Reuters via US News).

20 Sep: Operation Vivaldi phase two retook Shandryholove, Derylove and Drobysheve; the 3rd Army Corps says 125 km² is now under its control, 50 km² recaptured, and Russia's Rubicon drone formation was withdrawn after heavy losses (Kyiv Independent).

timeline.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three-hour talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against both capitals.
Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the pause declared during the US envoys' visit.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.
A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, halting processing for several weeks, Reuters reported citing industry sources.
Ukraine struck the Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa and the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara overnight, both more than 900 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, causing fires.
Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly, said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and urged trilateral talks with Putin at the G20 in Miami.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing two in Kyiv and damaging a maternity hospital, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow seeks peace rather than a temporary ceasefire, effectively rejecting the limited energy truce Ukraine had offered at the UN.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested watch area is borne out locally. On 20 Sep the 3rd Army Corps reported Vivaldi's second phase had retaken Shandryholove, Derylove and Drobysheve by moving assault groups through ravines for surprise, and on 23 Sep ISW noted the Russian defence ministry amplifying unfounded encirclement claims as cognitive warfare, so deception is contested in the information space as much as on the ground. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating holds: on 23 Sep Russia sent 161 drones, half jet-powered, of which 122 were downed, and on 24 Sep 282 drones with three ballistic waves, of which Zelensky said only 60% of ballistic missiles over Kyiv were intercepted. Finland's 24 Sep plea to Musk for Starlink over Russia shows the counter is now sought at the launcher.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the corps claims robots ran 15,700 missions, moved 3,300 tonnes and covered 90% of frontline evacuations, with kamikaze ground robots air-dropped 10 km behind Russian lines (24 Sep, single source). With the Kremlin rejecting an energy truce on 24 Sep and Ukraine reportedly reaching Perm on 25 Sep (single source), both sustainment systems stay under repeated targeting, and dispersed support preserves tempo only where robotic logistics are dense.

changes: 25 Sep: EU foreign policy chief Kallas told the two-state alliance meeting that Gaza progress is 'far too limited', with strikes continuing and humanitarian needs acute (Anadolu).

24 Sep: An Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle in al-Baidar south-west of Gaza City killed one man; a second strike hit the vehicle carrying his body near the Sheikh Ajleen pier, wounding relatives; two more were killed in central Gaza at al-Zahra and al-Zawaida (WAFA, Arab News). Health authorities count 73,922 killed since October 2023 and 1,408 since the ceasefire (single source for the ceasefire figure).

24 Sep: Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are 'the biggest lie of the century', called attacking Iran an easy decision and dismissed settler violence, without setting out ceasefire implementation steps (PBS, Al Jazeera).

24 Sep: Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem reiterated readiness to implement the Board of Peace roadmap, demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of international forces, and accused Mladenov of failing to pressure Israel (Palestinian Information Center, Al Jazeera).
24 Sep: Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies threaten the 'very life and existence' of Palestinians and described West Bank settlement as a 'colonial plan' (Al Jazeera).

23 Sep: The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament ('not bound by a calendar'), the same day Israeli strikes killed at least seven including Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan in al-Mawasi (Al Jazeera, Jerusalem Post).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
An Israeli-backed raid in Gaza City detained the head of Hamas's internal security service; airstrikes covering the withdrawal killed at least five Palestinians, including two children.
Kosovo signed a Participating Country Agreement for the International Stabilization Force in Pristina, while Board of Peace envoy Mladenov admitted implementation was 'not there yet'.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in al-Mawasi killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Hamas said it was ready to implement the roadmap and demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of the international force.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested watch area is borne out by method rather than scale. On 23 Sep a strike in al-Mawasi killed finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan, and on 24 Sep a vehicle south-west of Gaza City was struck twice, the second time while carrying the first victim's body (WAFA, single source). The 600-metre tunnel found on 23 Sep crossing the Yellow Line shows the network still moves under the line, so both sides are adapting within existing methods. On persistent ISR and precision strike versus civilian protection and legitimacy, the Contested status is confirmed at the strategic-information level: Netanyahu spent his 24 Sep UN speech rebutting the genocide charge rather than describing implementation, Abbas the same day called Israeli policy a threat to Palestinian existence, and on 25 Sep Kallas said Gaza progress is 'far too limited'. With 1,408 killed since the truce (single source), targeting freedom carries a rising legitimacy cost.

On humanitarian access versus operational control, the Established watch area holds but access is a bargaining chip: the Board of Peace's $2.4bn plan (23 Sep) is conditioned on disarmament with no calendar, Hamas on 24 Sep demanded the technocratic committee and ISF be let in, and Kerem Shalom offloading fell to 77% (OCHA, 11 Sep). Entry control, not capacity, governs endurance.

items.whyNow: Iran put a written road map on the table on 23 Sep (60-day regionwide ceasefire, phased Hormuz reopening, end of the blockade) and on 25 Sep its security chief gave Washington four to five days to accept it 'completely and all at once', while Reuters reported the two sides exploring a phased Hormuz-for-blockade deal and the Senate failed 49–50 to curb the war. The Strait remains effectively closed, a bulk carrier was hit on 23 Sep with one crew killed, and Singapore's crude route runs through the contested waters.
changes: 25 Sep: SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei said 'Talk is enough… Now we act', giving Washington four to five days to meet Iran's conditions 'completely and all at once' (declared commitment to diplomacy, negotiation timeline, sanctions relief, end of operations on all fronts) and warning that neighbours cooperating in aviation denial would see their airports closed; Rubio played down UNGA contacts as preliminary (Gulf News, Iran International).

24 Sep: Reuters sources said US and Iranian negotiators, mediated by Qatar, were exploring a staged deal in which Iran reopens Hormuz in return for an end to the US blockade, with neither side willing to give up leverage first; Pezeshkian told Fox News it is 'America that must choose' whether to end the war (US News/Reuters, Rappler).

24 Sep: The Senate failed 49–50 to advance the Iran war-powers resolution, with Collins, Murkowski, Paul and Tillis crossing and Fetterman opposing; Netanyahu told the UNGA that most of Hezbollah's arsenal was destroyed and that striking Iran was 'one of the easiest decisions' (CBS News, Times of Israel).

24 Sep: Saudi air defences intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Yanbu and Khamis Mushait as the Houthis claimed dozens of missiles and drones at Jazan; Brent settled at $103.08 on 23 Sep and traded near $106 on 24 Sep (Bloomberg, Washington Times, GlobalSecurity).

23 Sep: Iran handed the US a written road map through Qatari, Pakistani and Egyptian mediators: a regionwide ceasefire of up to 60 days, phased reopening of Hormuz, lifting of the blockade, a halt to attacks on Arab neighbours and a negotiating timeline; the same day the bulk carrier Cape Dao was struck by an unknown projectile off Musandam, left on fire and adrift, with one seafarer killed (The National, UKMTO, straits.live).

23 Sep: Pezeshkian told the UNGA Iran rejects 'the language of force' but is open to dialogue, calling Trump's annihilation threat bullying; the Iranian military called the threat 'strategic desperation'; Colombia's severance of ties with Iran and IRGC terrorist designation took effect 19 Sep, following Peru on 1 Sep (Al Jazeera, CNBC, BNO News).

timeline.text: The US and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lifted the US naval blockade, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and opened a 60-day negotiating period.
After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.
US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people, including five at a wedding in Kuhestak; the IRGC answered with missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait.
After the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.
Witkoff and Kushner held three hours of Qatari-mediated indirect talks with Iran's foreign minister in New York, as Trump told the UN he could 'annihilate' Iran absent a deal.

Iran handed the US a written road map for a 60-day regionwide ceasefire, phased reopening of Hormuz and an end to the blockade, while the bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit off Musandam and one seafarer was killed.
Reuters reported US and Iranian negotiators exploring a staged Hormuz-for-blockade deal, hours after the Senate failed 49–50 to advance a resolution to end the war.
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei gave Washington four to five days to accept Tehran's conditions all at once, saying the Strait stays closed otherwise and threatening neighbours' airports.

text: On long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence, the Established and Contested watch area is quiet on the direct axis and live on the proxy axis. No Iranian ballistic launches at host states or coalition strikes on Iranian territory were reported for 15 days to 24 Sep (single source), yet on 24 Sep Saudi defences intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Yanbu and Khamis Mushait. The interception burden has shifted to a Gulf partner's own systems. On maritime chokepoint disruption versus energy-route resilience, nothing has changed in kind: one transit was recorded on 20 Sep against a baseline of about 85, the Cape Dao was struck on 23 Sep with one seafarer killed and no attribution, and Brent was back above $106 on 24 Sep. The 23 Sep road map's 'phased reopening' makes the strait the bargaining currency, so resilience now turns on sequencing rather than mine clearance.

On deterrence versus proxy and deniable escalation, the Rising watch area is borne out. Unattributed projectiles on 21 and 23 Sep and the Houthi campaign on Saudi Red Sea ports ran on while Tehran negotiated, and on 25 Sep Rezaei paired a four-to-five-day ultimatum with a threat to close neighbours' airports. Deniable pressure and open coercion of third states now run alongside the phased-deal track reported on 24 Sep; adaptability stays High.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested watch area holds at low intensity while the ground shifts beneath it. The IDF said on 14–15 Sep that Hezbollah is re-entering pockets of the Yellow Line its troops never occupied, and that it answers with air, artillery and engineer fire rather than ground troops (single source); on 24 Sep artillery and airstrikes again covered Kfara, Beit Yahoun, Shaqra and Mansouri with no reported cross-border launch. The ceasefire survives in name because neither side wants the other's form of fight. On precision strike versus escalation control, restraint is thinning at the edges: UNIFIL counted on 22 Sep about 30 Israeli positions including eight fortified bases, a Lebanese source said the line's coordinates change daily (single source), and the 18 Sep Deir Mimas standoff was settled by tanks and stun grenades before the technical committee was consulted.

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger is closer. Beirut told the UN on 24 Sep it wants a mandated monitoring presence and no vacuum after UNIFIL, reportedly after a six-month extension request stalled (single source), and Salam told Pezeshkian that Lebanon will not be an arena for others' fights. Monitoring capacity is contracting as reconstitution inside the zone is reported; adaptability stays Medium, the learning being how a fires-only response polices a line it does not hold.

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.
Thai spokesman Prapas Sornchaidee warned of a full military response if Cambodian troops attacked near Chong Chom, while touring an O'Smach scam compound with ASEAN observers.
Cambodia and Thailand delivered opening statements in Singapore before a UNCLOS Annex V conciliation commission on their overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.
The first Singapore conciliation session closed with Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; the process is expected to take about a year.
The Thai army said Cambodia agreed to fill a trench and remove barbed wire at Hill 450 near Chong Sa-ngam in Si Sa Ket after coordination talks.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Hun Manet told an international anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh that Thailand weaponises scam crackdowns to occupy Cambodian territory; Thailand replied the next day that O'Smach was seized as a military base and urged real cooperation.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving reading holds in kinetic terms: between 11 and 25 Sep no exchange of fire was reported, the Hill 450 trench was resolved by liaison on 17 Sep (single source), and a live-feed headline about Thai tanks destroying a Cambodian casino traces to the December 2025 fighting, not a new action. Incidents are now symbolic, such as the Buddha statue placed at Phnom Beng on 18 Sep and protested on 22 Sep, which test restraint without offering a casus belli. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger conditions are still unmet, but the pattern is one of units and ministries creating facts: walls in Chanthaburi and Sa Kaeo, occupation of O'Smach justified since 23-24 Sep as a scam-compound seizure, and Cambodian counter-framing that anti-scam cooperation is being weaponised. Observers accompany rather than restrain.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the background-monitor status is borne out: the maritime dispute is being channelled into UNCLOS conciliation, whose second round in The Hague next month both foreign ministers on 24 Sep described as a shift to legal substance, while the land dispute is fought in forums, at the UNGA and in a nationalist online culture war. Adaptability remains Low: containment through law and rhetoric, not resolution, and no bilateral border committee has met this year.

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.
US-backed talks between Delcy Rodríguez's interim government and an opposition delegation led by Dinorah Figuera opened in Caracas, with Jorge Rodríguez heading the government side.
The White House announced 100-year concessions on 17 Venezuelan oil fields to North American Blue Energy Partners, with the US government taking a 35 percent stake.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere struck a go-fast vessel on Caribbean narco-trafficking routes, killing four, in the 70th US counter-cartel maritime strike.
Trump held a pull-aside meeting with interim President Delcy Rodríguez at a UN General Assembly reception, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger for this watch area has still not fired: US action stays at sea, and the only new military move in the window is preparatory, the redeployment of MQ-9 Reapers from Africa to SOUTHCOM reported on 18 Sep for operations that Hegseth has framed as joint with Colombia. The escalation risk therefore sits in legal and political exposure, with the UN rapporteur's findings from 22 Sep still unanswered. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out by continuity: the 70th strike on 19 Sep killed four and raised the toll to 234, yet strikes have thinned to roughly one every ten days, which suggests either fewer go-fast transits or a shift to interdiction; no spillover, displacement or armed confrontation was reported.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is strongly supported and now drives the item. Rodríguez's 23 Sep UN pledge of elections without a date, the removal of a Telemundo reporter who asked when (single source), Machado's seventh blocked return on 22 Sep and a 24 Sep Caracas rally demanding a timetable (single source) show the government sourcing legitimacy from Washington, debt talks and oil deals while the opposition sources it from the street and a July 2027 date. Adaptability stays Medium: the electoral calendar, not force, is the contested ground.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025.

India and Pakistan each summon the other's charge d'affaires over the collision; Pakistan calls it 'belligerent Indian action', India calls the Pakistani ship's conduct 'unacceptable and unprofessional'.
Two Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammad militants are killed overnight in 'Operation Sohan' in the Majalta forests of Udhampur, Jammu, and a suspected over-ground worker is detained.
India rejects Pakistan's version of the warship collision as 'the usual prevarication', insisting INS Kolkata was on routine surveillance in international waters.

India signs a Rs 810.79 crore contract for 160 satellite-guided Smart Anti-Airfield Weapons and rejects the OIC Contact Group's Kashmir communiqué, telling the group to 'counsel Pakistan' on terrorism.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans and demands it vacate the parts of Jammu and Kashmir it holds, as New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status held without a kinetic test: after the 15 Sep Arabian Sea collision each side settled into competing narratives, India's 18 Sep 'usual prevarication' rebuttal being the last move, and no Line of Control fire was reported between 18 and 25 Sep. Signalling shifted to procurement and exercises: the 23 Sep contract for 160 satellite-guided anti-airfield glide bombs (deliveries 2027–29) and Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur from 26 Sep with US F-35s keep India's stand-off airfield-strike option visible to Rawalpindi. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established rating is borne out by rhetoric rather than casualties: India's 24 Sep UNHRC reply tied Pakistan to 'exporting terror', its 23 Sep rejection of the OIC communiqué told the group to 'counsel Pakistan', and Jammu search operations continued against an estimated 25 militants (22 Sep, single source).

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested edge is being argued in Geneva, New York and Gilgit rather than tested: Rubio's 23 Sep remark that the international system cannot address a potential India–Pakistan conflict, and a 25 Sep Pakistani strategic-stability workshop framing Indian force posture as destabilising (single source), show Washington and Islamabad treating a repeat crisis as plausible. Adaptability remains High on paper but unexercised; the window's adaptation is India's turn to lawfare and stand-off munitions.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government at the parliament complex in Naypyitaw.
Min Aung Hlaing offers peace talks to armed groups with a 100-day deadline ending 31 July; the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and National Unity Government reject it.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.
An Air Force strike on a truck rest stop at Sattawkone village on the Mandalay-Myitkyina highway in Indaw Township kills two civilians and destroys two trucks.
Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand, Zaw Zaw Soe, for questioning over migrant-worker transfers and passports issued to anti-regime figures; Bangkok says it was not informed.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds and airpower keeps substituting for stalled ground movement: the 4 Sep Rakhine offensive recovered no ground, and by 20 Sep the regime had instead staged a 180-vehicle, 1,000-troop column with MLRS, drones and signal jammers at Saw Township to reopen the Mindat–Kanpetlet axis (single source), while jets struck a school at Kyathaungseik on 19 Sep (single source) and a highway rest stop near Indaw on 23 Sep. Ground force generation, not sorties, remains the binding constraint. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out on both sides: KIA drone attacks on the Bhamo river convoy since late August let only seven of fifteen vessels through, and the regime is layering Pechora-2M, Pantsir-S1 and Chinese Skyfend counter-drone systems and now packs jammers into columns, so repeatable effect depends on whether resistance FPV cells can out-cycle that protection.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is confirmed by the regime's own reach fraying outward: the 24 Sep recall of its ambassador to Thailand over migrant-worker and passport allegations (single source) and Bangladesh's 25 Sep UNGA demand for Rohingya return show labour and refugee corridors becoming bargaining objects, which undercuts the normalisation drive with ASEAN neighbours.
